action_criteria.rationale: An 11-month magnetic gait with urge incontinence and an outside report of enlarged ventricles needs an MRI that measures the ventricles and excludes obstruction before CSF is removed.

action_criteria.rationale: Normal-pressure CSF and an objective tap response support probable iNPH and predict shunt benefit.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not perform the large-volume lumbar tap before brain MRI has excluded a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus

Do not diagnose iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone: the diagnosis needs the clinical syndrome (gait disturbance with cognitive or urinary symptoms) and supportive imaging, with no other cause explaining them [Relkin_2005]
Do not attribute the cognitive decline to Alzheimer's disease on the family history alone, given the gait-first course, the executive profile with cued recall and the tap response
Do not attribute the new gait disorder to the prior cervical disease when the cervical MRI shows no compression and the exam has no upper motor neuron signs
Do not attribute the syndrome to normal ageing or deconditioning once the ventriculomegaly and the tap response are documented
required_recommendations: Refer to neurosurgery for CSF shunting with a programmable valve, on the basis of the tap-test improvement of 21% in TUG at 24 hours, the DESH MRI with an acute callosal angle and normal-pressure CSF [Nakajima_2021]
Review gabapentin as a contributor to unsteadiness and cognitive slowing and keep the dose unchanged across the tap test
Confirm euthyroid status on levothyroxine (TSH and free T4) so that hypothyroidism is excluded as a contributor
Falls-prevention measures (physiotherapy, home assessment, walking aid) while awaiting surgery

avoided_actions.rationale: She has no episodes suggesting seizures, so an EEG cannot separate iNPH from its mimics.
Her falls are mechanical, with no syncope or palpitations, so an ECG does not inform the gait work-up.
There is no syncope, murmur or embolic event, so echocardiography has no role in this work-up.
An MRI is available and shows DESH, the callosal angle and the aqueduct better than CT.
The falls are not syncopal, so rhythm monitoring has no diagnostic role here.
Molecular or advanced imaging does not change the iNPH decision, which rests on MRI and the tap test
A full neuropsychological battery is not needed for the iNPH decision; the bedside screen and timed gait measures are
Normal-pressure CSF with a normal cell count in a chronic afebrile gait syndrome gives no indication for prion, inflammatory or infectious assays.

differential.key_features: The cervical MRI shows a patent canal at C5-C6 with normal cord signal, and the exam has no clonus, Babinski or lower-limb hyperreflexia, so recurrent myelopathy does not explain the non-spastic shuffling gait.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: White matter change is only Fazekas grade 1, too little to explain the gait and cognitive decline.
Mild leg tone increase without rest tremor, rigidity in the arms or bradykinesia, and a gait that improved after CSF removal, argue against parkinsonism.
Her mother had Alzheimer's disease, but free recall normalises with cues, the hippocampi are MTA 1 and the gait disorder came first, which does not suggest Alzheimer's disease as the main cause.

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: DESH with tight convexity sulci, an acute callosal angle and a tap response argue against atrophy ex vacuo.
There is no history of head trauma, subarachnoid haemorrhage, meningitis or intracranial surgery; the only operation was on the cervical spine.

key_clinical_evidence: An 11-month insidious decline from age 65 with a magnetic gait, urge incontinence and executive slowing, with no antecedent trauma, haemorrhage or meningitis, meets the clinical criteria for probable iNPH [Relkin_2005]
MRI shows Evans index 0.32 with DESH, an acute callosal angle (88 degrees), enlarged temporal horns and a patent aqueduct [Nakajima_2021]
Opening pressure 16 cmH2O with normal CSF content; after 40 mL was removed, TUG improved 21% at 24 hours (24 to 19 s) and the 10-metre walk 18% [Nakajima_2021]
Tap-test sensitivity is 26% to 61% with a PPV of 73% to 100%; the positive tap supports shunting [Marmarou_2005]
The previous cervical gait was spastic; the new gait is not, the exam has no upper motor neuron signs and the cervical MRI shows no compression or cord signal change
TSH and free T4 are normal on levothyroxine, so hypothyroidism is not a contributor; gabapentin 900 mg/day can add unsteadiness and should be kept constant across the tap

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain imaging must exclude a mass or obstructive hydrocephalus before CSF is removed [Relkin_2005]

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive gait instability, 'brain fog,' and urinary incontinence for 11 months; worried about Alzheimer's disease because of her mother's history

past_medical_history: Cervical spondylosis with prior cervical discectomy (C5-C6, 3 years ago)

patient.history_present_illness: A 66-year-old right-handed woman with hypothyroidism, hypertension, and a history of cervical discectomy at C5-C6 three years ago (with good postoperative recovery and only residual mild right arm paresthesias on gabapentin) was admitted for evaluation of progressive gait, cognitive and urinary symptoms. Over the past 11 months she has developed three progressive symptoms: (1) Gait instability — her husband describes a 'magnetic' gait with small shuffling steps that has progressively worsened; she has fallen twice. The gait change concerns her orthopedic surgeon because it is different from the gait abnormality she had from her cervical disease preoperatively, which was more spastic. (2) Cognitive decline — she describes 'brain fog,' difficulty multitasking, and forgetting where she put objects. Her family history of Alzheimer's (mother) makes her very anxious about this symptom. (3) Urinary urgency with occasional incontinence — she describes the need to rush to the bathroom and has had several near-miss accidents. A brain MRI obtained as an outpatient at an outside facility was reported as showing enlarged ventricles; the images are not available. The referring neurologist notes the prior cervical spine surgery as a potential alternative explanation for the gait change.
